#139055. Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1014 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.
  • According to recent reports, although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China.
  • The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.

According to recent reports, although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China. In a press release, however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.

The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

According to recent reports, among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ stated. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its users’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”.

Sources indicate that as the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of Newly introduced York Joseph Nocella Jr. remarked that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage manufacturer called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

One of the stolen ideas was the design of a T-Mobile robot called “Tappy,” which helped the US firm “assess the responsiveness of touch screens by mimicking a human touch,” the DOJ said. To copy the design, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement, then sent photos and technical details back to China. Even bolder, when that intel was deemed insufficient, “a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DOJ said.

Huawei’s tactics weren’t always sophisticated, but they were effective, the DOJ mentioned, building into “a long-running conspiracy to steal intellectual property of US companies.” At trade highlights and tours of rivals’ facilities, Huawei employees would pretend to “get lost,” the DOJ said, so they could wander into restricted areas and take photos of hardware, The Fresh York Times reported.

Huawei engineers would also sometimes hide their activity by spelling words backwards. For example, Huawei was able to copy the source code used on Cisco routers—which the DOJ said was “identified as the ‘crown jewel’ of Cisco technology”—by taking notes in which they spelled Cisco as “ocsic.” Another time, the DOJ noted that a Huawei employee was caught “photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment” while wearing a badge that falsely identified him as an employee of “Weihua.”.

During the trial, Meredith Arfa, a federal prosecutor, noted that Huawei employees were sometimes paid bonuses for their crimes, since the theft was so integral to Huawei’s business model, NYT reported.

Roman Rozhavsky, the assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, noted that Huawei spent years expanding its international enterprise “through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of US companies and the rule of law.”.

Sources indicate that huawei has been banned from selling its tech in the US since 2019, so NYT noted that the guilty verdict is unlikely to rattle the company’s finances much. However, the financial penalties stemming from the verdict could be steep, as the DOJ explained that they include “criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution.”.

Sentencing is scheduled for September 14.

Huawei continues to deny any wrongdoing and rejects US claims that the Chinese Communist Party directed the thefts. NYT noted that Huawei’s investors have argued that the US fight is politically motivated and seeks to hobble “a Chinese initiative to build 5G networks around the world.”.

Industry observers note that outside the courthouse following the verdict, Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that it’s significant that the jury did not convict Huawei of racketeering charges or conspiracy to obstruct justice. According to Heberlig, the examples of US technology theft merely represented “isolated misconduct by manufacturer employees,” which inevitably happens in a company so large, with “hundreds of thousands of people.”.

Heberlig confirmed that Huawei planned to appeal and considered the jury’s opposition to racketeering charges to be a “profound rejection of the United States’ narratives about what Huawei is.”.

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hard-working manufacturer that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” Heberlig said.

After the verdict, China “lashed out” at the US, AFP reported. According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, the US is trying to use the ruling to “suppress” Huawei.

China “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” Guo said.

However, the FBI’s Rozhavsky suggested that even China, which frequently negotiates with Trump as the trade rivals continually clash, can’t spare Huawei from substantial penalties.

In a recent development, “This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation,” Rozhavsky mentioned. “No organization is too substantial, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the US and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

Recent findings suggest that this is a very welcome feature. One of the few things I genuinely like about email (other than it being a truly decentralized means of communication) is being able to schedule replies. I don't really need anyone to know that I'm actually hashing out an email to them late at night. I usually schedule it to send the next morning so I don't seem like someone who works too much even though I definitely work too much.

Recent findings suggest that whatsApp suggested some other ways scheduled messages might be useful, such as to wish someone luck just before a test or job interview, or to make sure they receive a happy birthday message right when it's midnight for them (especially if you're not in the same time zone). You'll be able to see all of the messages you've timed up to send in the future and delete them if you change your mind. WhatsApp said that, as with all other personal messages, scheduled messages are end-to-end encrypted, so only you and the recipient(s) can read them.

New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
  • The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
  • The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the newly introduced deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the newly introduced deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme.

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students.

Farage helps launch fresh campaign against the UK rejoining the EU.

According to recent reports, under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer stated: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements.".

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier.".

A strategy to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.

However, the UK will not be given voting rights.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.

Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also remarked it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

According to recent reports, several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham mentioned they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch stated Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

#139049. The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1808 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager.
  • According to recent reports, davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm.
  • The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

According to recent reports, davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a fresh way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows owners to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

Sources indicate that researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

In a recent development, davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”.

It has been revealed that davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he claims.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.

It has been revealed that A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, states Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”.

Sources indicate that in late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” notes George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Recent findings suggest that nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.

That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

Industry observers note that to get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”.

Recent findings suggest that the second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

Sources indicate that he’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

Recent findings suggest that at first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”.

Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he states.

Today, he indicates, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Sources indicate that curiously, he also indicates he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

It has been revealed that the phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” states Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology manufacturer that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The research team is right now planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful upcoming technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow owners to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he states.

According to recent reports, george hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”.

Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”.

Latest Update: Protests in Iraqi Kurdistan at looks for government in Baghdad to take over oil, border crossings

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.
  • They were responding to federal government plans unveiled earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.
  • Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had said the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.

They were responding to federal government plans unveiled earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had said the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.

According to state media reports, later on Thursday, Iraqi border forces closed two border crossings with Syria and Iran that had been administered by the Kurdish authorities.

Iraq's border forces commander told the Iraqi News Agency that the al-Waleed border crossing with Syria and the Bashta border crossing with Iran have been closed.

The plans marked an escalation in the long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities that have largely governed themselves since 1991, albeit with varying levels of recognition and authority.

Rival Kurdish parties joined forces for the large protests in the regional capital.

Protests were also reported to have spread to several other towns and cities beyond the capital.

Iraq's 2005 constitution, written following the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, formally recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But authorities in Erbil and Baghdad have remained in a tug of war over the control of land, oil and money ever since.

According to recent reports, tuesday's decision, which received backing from Iraq's Federal Supreme Court a day later, brings border crossing in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in four contested provinces — Kirkuk, Diyala, Salahuddin and Nineveh.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The Kurdish regional government's Cabinet said on Wednesday that the decision from Baghdad "violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan region," saying it represented "an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime.".

According to recent reports, prime Minister al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump, also dismissed Kirkuk's operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflected Iraq's "independent national will.".

Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani mentioned his government was "surprised" by al-Zaidi's decisions and called them "completely unacceptable.".

Iraq's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the authority of the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) only covered the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein.

Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week's orders.

The 2005 constitution tried to solve the fate of some of the disputed territories in the lands between the borders to Syria and Iran that are home to a host of ethnicities and communities but with Kurds generally the majority group.

Sources indicate that article 140 called for reversing Saddam-era policies of expelling Kurds and moving Arabs in, and called for a census and a referendum on whether the disputed regions should join the Kurdistan region. Neither was held.

Kurdish forces then gained more of the disputed territory after Iraqi forces were forced out by the so-called "Islamic State," with Kurdish pershmerga for subsequently reclaiming some of the land with some international assistance.

The oil-rich region is highly important to both administrations, in a country that relies on oil revenues for the vast majority of its public sector budget.

Internal political tensions within Iraqi Kurdistan have further complicated the problem in recent months, with the Federal Supreme Court hearing an ongoing challenge against the current government's legitimacy after a party withdrew from the coalition cabinet. But rival Kurdish political factions seem to have found common ground on this issue at least.

Industry observers note that the desktop is housed in a compact 35 liter mid-tower and the system comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F processor, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, a 1TB SSD and an NVIDIA RTX 5070 GPU with 12GB of vRAM. That right there is a pretty solid foundation for a mid-range gaming rig that can handle both 1080p and QHD gaming with ease (depending on the title of course). This offer is especially enticing when considering the cost of those individual components if you bought them separately.

It has been revealed that let's start with the CPU, and compare it against other listings on Amazon. If you search for an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F, that particular CPU is actually sold out at the time of writing, and the next closest processor is a Core Ultra 7 265 processor that's going for $365. Next, we can move on to 32GB of DDR5 RAM, which is similar to this 2 x 16GB Corsair Vengeance kit that's listed for $470. Finally, there's the RTX 5070 GPU which is right now going for between $910 and $980 on Amazon from a couple different OEMs.

So even if we take the cheapest price for each component, you're looking at a total cost of $1,745 for just the system's three most expensive pieces of hardware, which means you're basically getting a case, a PSU, fans, heatsinks and a 1TB SSD for $150 — and without the need to do any assembly. That's one of the best deals I've seen for a gaming PC in a while. To give you even more context, if you go to the official Dell/Alienware website, you can find an Aurora desktop with the exact same specs listed at around $2,600. This means we're looking at a potential savings of around $700 compared to its standard pricing.

Meanwhile, the rest of the system is pretty well equipped. It comes with a good selection of front IO including three USB-A, one USB-C and a 3.5mm audio jack. Around back, there's even more connectivity with a total of six additional USB connectors (two Type-C and four Type-A), 2.5 gigabit Ethernet, more audio jacks and even a SPDIF optical port. And on the inside, you get a motherboard with an Intel Z890 chipset with three PCIe slots and support for Wi-Fi 7. There's even a little window on its side panel so you can see the system's built-in RGB lighting and all those pricey components.

Industry observers note that however, anyone thinking about buying this system should be careful about reading too much into Amazon's listed specs. Details for this offer say the Aurora comes with a built-in optical drive, but I'm pretty sure that's a mistake. Furthermore, Amazon's page says the desktop comes with a 450-watt PSU, while other materials state the PC has a 500-watt power supply. Also, while you can configure an Aurora with water-cooling on Alienware's website, this particular model is merely air-cooled.

Regardless, if you've been caught off-guard by the rapid rise in PC components over the past year and a half and have been waiting for a system with a more reasonable price, this $1,900 Alienware Aurora desktop might be the deal you're looking for. Just don't wait too long because this offer seems poised to sell out fast.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba's social media posts have previously sparked diplomatic tensions.

The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.

The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.

The Ugandan government has yet to respond.

The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.

Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.

Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.

Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever.

The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter.

In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.

The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.

They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.

He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.

Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.

Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.

It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.

During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed.".

The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.

Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.

"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry stated in a statement on Wednesday.

"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".

The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".

It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.

In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.

In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.

The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.

In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

For the first time in years, he can handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, or a loved one's hand.

Davidson is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted, but he's the first to take it home and use it independently. Researchers hope his experiences will reveal how useful the technology really is in day-to-day life, and how it might affect his brain and nervous system.

Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers.
  • In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.
  • According to recent reports, we see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.

According to recent reports, we see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:.

According to recent reports, the second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

According to recent reports, much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:.

It has been revealed that I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

Such lessons are key because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki mentioned:.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

    The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Baaja) passed the Senate 62-33 and is now being debated in the House. The Baaja is a “permitting reform” bill that aims to reduce the time it takes federal agencies to approve major energy and infrastructure projects, like power lines, fossil fuel pipelines, natural gas plants and datacenters.

    NASA's DART mission left a stadium-sized crater in an asteroid, the ESA finds

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The ESA’s Hera mission has begun capturing images of the aftermath of DART’s impact.
    • In March, NASA revealed it successfully altered the orbit of Dimorphos and its parent asteroid Didymos around the Sun with its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and now thanks to latest images captured by the ESA's Hera spacecraft, we have a better idea of what that mission actually did to the smaller of the two asteroids.
    • The crater extends across the entire width of Dimorphos, according to Michel, yet it didn't alter the fields of boulders that cover the rest of the asteroid.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The ESA’s Hera mission has begun capturing images of the aftermath of DART’s impact.

    In March, NASA revealed it successfully altered the orbit of Dimorphos and its parent asteroid Didymos around the Sun with its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and now thanks to latest images captured by the ESA's Hera spacecraft, we have a better idea of what that mission actually did to the smaller of the two asteroids. The 2022 controlled crash created an "impact crater the size of a sports stadium," according to Patrick Michel, the Director of Research at France's National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Hera's principal investigator.

    The crater extends across the entire width of Dimorphos, according to Michel, yet it didn't alter the fields of boulders that cover the rest of the asteroid. Besides physically altering the surface of Dimorphos, the ESA found that the DART impact sent the asteroid tumbling in its new orbit. Hera also revealed that both Dimorphos and Didymos are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders.

    All of these new details were captured by Hera's monochrome Asteroid Framing Camera, multi-spectral Hyperscout H and JAXA-developed Thermal Infrared Imager from about 25 to 30km away from the asteroids, the ESA says.

    In a recent development, "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli said. "Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.".

    Recent findings suggest that NASA and other space agencies are exploring altering asteroids' orbits as one way of protecting the Earth from potentially dangerous future impacts. In December, the ESA aims to move Hera closer to Dimorphos and Didymos to capture even higher-resolution images of the impact site. In January, Hera will also deploy shoebox-sized CubeSats to collect other types of data. The Juventas CubeSat, created by a Luxembourg-led research team, will use radar to probe the asteroid's interior and eventually land on its surface. An Italian-led team will use the other CubeSat, Milani, to prospect asteroid dust and other surrounding materials.

    • It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday.
    • Recent findings suggest that rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province.
    • Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The flooded mine is in Bogor in West Java.

    It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.

    Recent findings suggest that rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.

    Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.

    Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.

    Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.

    "We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.

    "The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely.".

    Rescuers have been working day and night to find survivors in the flooded mine shaft.

    Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.

    Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high â spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.

    This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have stated the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.

    On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.

    But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.

    In a recent development, "[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he mentioned, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.

    "It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time.".

    Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.

    Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, remarked that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".

    "As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.

    In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.

    Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.

    But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common â whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.

    Relatives of the missing Bogor miners have been waiting near the site for news of their loved ones.

    Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.

    Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.

    There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.

    Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".

    "Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it.".

    The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.

    "This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," stated Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.

    According to recent reports, "We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.

    "Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going.".

    According to recent reports, as rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.

    More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.

    As she waits for news of her father, Rani claims: "I hope he's found soon.".

    Etsy clarifies AI terms after seller backlash

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (432 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the firm to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.
    • In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the tech giant’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.
    • In a recent development, “Our recent terms patch was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the firm to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

    In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the tech giant’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.

    In a recent development, “Our recent terms patch was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”.

    Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the organization had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”.

    He stated he still looks on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

    “I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he said. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”.

    He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

    “This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he said.

    Industry observers note that the fracas began earlier this month, when the company first proposed fresh contractual language. The updated terms read:.

    As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”.

    Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

    Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

    “Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the manufacturer’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”.

    For years, Etsy has been notoriously poor at enforcing its own rules, not only regarding AI but also the official prohibitions on selling sex toys, pornography, and even purported witchcraft spells.

    #139026. A New Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1328 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

    A New Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.
    • To rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build new data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia.
    • An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German company Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a new breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.

    To rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build new data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia. But logistical challenges, a scarcity of key components, and a swell of anti-data center protests are getting in the way.

    An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German company Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a new breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.

    It has been revealed that whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data by shuffling electrons around, photonic processors use waves of light. Because light doesn’t generate heat as it travels and allows more data to be processed simultaneously, photonic processors supposedly consume less energy and require minimal cooling—one of the largest sources of cost for data centers.

    The aim isn’t to replace GPUs with photonic processors, but to run them side-by-side. Whilst GPUs excel at grinding through masses of additions and multiplications—linear math—photonic processors are best suited to complex, nonlinear calculations.

    Few photonic processors are running inside data centers today. But Q.ANT recently rolled out its chips to facilities operated by cloud tech giant IONOS as part of a pilot program. It says that more than 30 teams of engineers are now developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.

    Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, WIRED spoke with Michael Förtsch, founder and CEO of Q.ANT. We discussed the energy bottlenecks constraining AI development, how photonic processors differ from regular chips, and the challenges Q.ANT faces in trying to popularize a new class of hardware.

    This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining the problem Q.ANT is aiming to solve? Why does the world need photonic processors to run AI models?

    Michael Förtsch: The overall problem is the cost generated by the huge amount of energy consumption.

    If you compute the way we think light should be used—not as a direct replacement for a GPU, but as a coprocessor—you basically have a latest processor that takes care of the heavy math.

    Industry observers note that the cost driver today is the access to the memory. The less data you need in order to complete a job, the more efficient and better your system. We execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps. This saves a bunch of data—or memory access points.

    How would you explain to the layperson how photonic computing works? How can light be used to perform mathematical computations?

    Light is a wave. What is a wave? A sine function. [The sine function is a mathematical rule that, when plotted to a graph, produces a smooth repeating wave. —Editor] If I want to model something that’s round in shape with only linear functions, I need an infinite amount of data points and lines in order to describe something very simple: a circle. If I have the sine function at hand, because light is a wave, I need two points and I have already described the circle in all its beauty.

    Light is very, very gifted to operate on complicated equations.

    What distinguishes the type of problem best left to regular chips from problems that should be delegated to photonic processors?

    The Nvidia H200 GPU is a masterpiece of technology. It’s art. It’s truly hard to attack it in its homeground. But light has strengths where the GPU is weak—and vice versa.

    In a recent development, linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.

    We believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures and videos: image recognition, segmentation, and generation. Then, everything that’s related to robotics and physical AI.

    What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency tied to using photonic processors alongside GPUs for AI tasks?

    In a recent development, I’m not saying photonic computing will come for free. But I see that photonic computing, in combination with [CPUs and GPUs], can bring you a lot more artificial intelligence at a fraction of the energy.

    It has been revealed that under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.

    Can any task run on photonic hardware by default, or do they need to be configured in a certain way?

    There’s no need to learn a different language than C++ or Python. And you can already execute [preexisting] code on our machines.

    Recent findings suggest that but if you take something that has been optimized for a GPU only, you should not expect that automatically things will run faster. You have to do some adaptations.

    In a recent development, it’s a chicken and egg problem, right? Until developers are building models to run on this type of processor, it’s going to be difficult to sell them to cloud providers. Equally, until photonic processors are available for people to use, it’s going to be tough to convince developers to design for them.

    Whether it’s photonic or any other processor technology, it will need time to get the credibility and trust that’s needed for a company like Google to build data center infrastructure around it.

    That’s the reason we chose to go into data centers with proof of concept systems, to validate that photonic computing is robust enough to withstand that environment.

    We want to invite the world to compute on our systems. We are building a latest chicken, so you can start producing eggs. Let’s find out together whether they’re tasty or not.

    What else should I understand about why photonic processors are not already widely in use?

    If hypothetically we received an order of 100,000 [photonic processors], we at Q.ANT are ready, but I’m not sure about the suppliers.

    Industry observers note that hardware is not software. On the assembly side, it will need [time] before we have the same robust supply chain as the semiconductor world.

    Do you expect to suffer from the same problem as other hardware challengers in securing capacity with the big chip manufacturers?

    Sources indicate that [To produce Q.ANT chips] you only need 90 nanometer node technology, from the 2000s. A lot of foundries already use this capability to produce chips that are super cheap. With this technology, you can use the same line to produce high-performance chips with a much higher street price, without massive upfront investment in your assets.

    That resonates well with the industry.

    Are Q.ANT processors built to function alongside a particular brand of GPUs—say, Nvidia or AMD—or are they totally agnostic?

    In a recent development, there’s no need to go single-sided with a particular GPU. We want to have the freedom to cooperate with any of them.

    Either way, we are not competitive to GPUs, we complete their function set.

    Can you imagine a future in which AI models run entirely on photonic processors, or will they always be a sidekick?

    Recent findings suggest that if we see an opportunity in five years to attack the GPU as well, we would not be shy about taking it. But at the same time, I do not know what workloads in five years are going to be like.

    It depends on the architecture of future AI models, you mean?

    Could the chance to perform certain calculations more cheaply with photonic processors change the way that AI engineers design future models?

    The core message is that we need to do something to fight the energy cost in the AI stack.

    That’s where we see the future of AI: very data-optimized models that allow for tasks of the same quality, but at a fraction of the energy—and therefore a fraction of the operating cost.

    On farewell trip, Steinmeier calls for more investment in Africa

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • "My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was key to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," noted Frank-Walter Steinmeier during his final official trip to Africa.
    • According to recent reports, "For me personally, things have come full circle today," the president added during his opening remarks at the German-African Business Summit in Ghana.
    • This week, in addition to Ghana, he visited Cote d'Ivoire and Kenya with a business delegation from Germany.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    "My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was key to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," noted Frank-Walter Steinmeier during his final official trip to Africa. Over the course of 20 years, as president and before that as foreign minister, the veteran politician has made 30 trips to African countries.

    According to recent reports, "For me personally, things have come full circle today," the president added during his opening remarks at the German-African Business Summit in Ghana. He was alluding to the first German-African business summit in Berlin in 2015, which Steinmeier opened while he was still foreign minister in the administration of former Chancellor Angela Merkel.

    This week, in addition to Ghana, he visited Cote d'Ivoire and Kenya with a business delegation from Germany.

    A lot has happened since 2015, Steinmeier said. And yet: "We are still far from where we could be." Addressing Germany's business community, he said, "Be curious, take risks.".

    It has been revealed that as the applause rang out after the speech, Jude Numfor, who works for the energy company REI in Cameroon, smiled. He too sees German companies as too risk-averse.

    "When the Chinese come, they say 'let's do it,' and the Germans say 'let's prepare it'," he told DW.

    Meanwhile, Africa's economy is growing rapidly. German-African foreign trade rose by 10.5% in 2025 to €63.4 billion ($69.4 billion). Africa's trade with the Asia-Pacific region is growing more slowly, but the absolute figures are also significantly higher.

    This reveals there is a great deal of potential in Africa's markets — especially in light of the emerging African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which encompasses most of the continent.

    When it comes to direct investment, German companies are more hesitant than others — a trend observed not only by Numfor: China, Turkey and the Gulf states are willing to take on more risk and are pushing into these markets.

    The Chinese, in particular, are offering large loans to build key rail lines and ports, and they are buying up mines and raw materials in Africa. But since they usually bring their own low-wage labor force with them, China's investments often create few local jobs.

    Sources indicate that but such jobs would be the linchpin of Africa's future. In Kenya alone, 1 million young people enter the labor market each year; in Nigeria, the number is even higher, and some experts therefore anticipate even more irregular migration to Europe in the coming years.

    Germany has noted there is a need for action: It supports vocational training in Africa and, for several years now, has also been allowing skilled workers to emigrate to Germany from Africa.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Sources indicate that during his trip, Steinmeier also visited educational institutions such as the vocational school for mechanics and industrial maintenance in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire. In Kenya, he spoke with President William Ruto about the implications of the 2024 bilateral migration and mobility partnership and more opportunities for language and vocational training.

    There are now around 9,500 Kenyans working in Germany, and nearly 1,300 in vocational training. "We want to open up opportunities for young people and create regular, fair and orderly pathways for labor and skilled worker migration," Steinmeier noted in Nairobi.

    Vocational training is said to be most effective where businesses and factories are being established.

    According to recent reports, "A very favorable window of opportunity for investment is currently opening up in Africa," remarked Fritz Audebert, CEO of ICUnet, a company that advises German firms on investment projects worldwide. "We've noticed a shift over the past two years or so, driven in part by geopolitical changes, the complicated situation in China, and most recently the war in Iran.".

    Recent findings suggest that "More and more companies are beginning to understand this," Audebert added. "While there are reservations, we're seeing a similar sentiment to that regarding India." What's newly introduced is that small and medium-sized enterprises from Germany are also showing interest in Africa.

    During the trip, Audebert was particularly impressed by Cote d'Ivoire, as he remarked, "because of the ministers' high level of expertise." The country is the world's largest cocoa exporter and possesses important raw materials. "You can work well with this potential," he said.

    Members of the business delegation accompanying Steinmeier also agreed that the German automotive industry must focus more on the African market.

    "The middle class is growing in cities, and with it, the demand for mobility," said Audebert.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Markus Thill, president of Bosch Africa, confirms there is a considerable market for simple, gas- and diesel-driven cars. "Based on the auto industry's experience, we know that households worldwide with an annual income of €10,000 or more can afford a upcoming car," said Thill. This would mean that potentially 5-10 million new cars per year could be built and sold in Africa.

    Instead, "we export millions of old used cars to Africa that would no longer be eligible for registration in Europe," he said.

    Even though the focus of the trip was on the economy, "we shouldn't limit our view to that," Steinmeier remarked at the end of his trip. Germany maintains a reliable political partnership with Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana and Kenya.

    "These are three countries with which we cooperate closely on the international stage, and in that sense, visiting them now was the right and deliberate choice," he mentioned.

    When asked to take stock of his 30 trips to African countries undertaken during his political career, Steinmeier said: "There is not one Africa, but many, and there are also very different, uneven developments there." This fact, he concluded, needs to be "communicated even more effectively" in Germany.

    This article was originally written in German.

    💡 Key Takeaways
