    The judge has preliminarily sided with ABC, rejecting the FCC’s efforts to dismiss the case.﻿.

    According to recent reports, US District Judge Loren AliKhan has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses in a preliminary injunction, and rejected its efforts to dismiss ABC’s First Amendment lawsuit. ABC has accused the FCC of violating its free speech rights and claims the agency “waged a retaliatory campaign” against the network over content it broadcast. In her ruling the judge noted that the network was “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim.”.

    Although Disney, ABC’s parent company, wasn’t set to renew its broadcast licenses until 2028, last April the FCC ordered the network to file for an early license renewal claiming it was part of an investigation into Disney’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusivity. The FCC’s move came a day after President Donald Trump demanded ABC fire late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel following a skit about Melania Trump.

    In response to the FCC’s order, Disney and ABC sued the agency in August and accused the FCC of “punishing ABC for its speech” by threatening its broadcast licenses. The preliminary injunction issued by the judge on Wednesday prohibits the FCC from taking any further action in the early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses and noted that the network had shown that the court’s intervention in the agency’s actions was in the public interest.

    Sources indicate that ”No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” the judge wrote. “But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”.

    Industry News: Workers at GTA 6 studio Rockstar Games vote overwhelmingly against union recognition

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (451 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union will continue to organize, however.
    • Recent findings suggest that rockstar Games workers in the UK have overwhelmingly voted against a union recognition effort, with three-quarters rejecting an agreement with the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union.
    • According to recent reports, over 93 percent of Rockstar workers across offices in Edinburgh, Leeds, Lincoln, Dundee and London took part in the two-week ballot.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union will continue to organize, however.

    Recent findings suggest that rockstar Games workers in the UK have overwhelmingly voted against a union recognition effort, with three-quarters rejecting an agreement with the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union. The vote took place at the same time the organization released Grand Theft Auto 6, which smashed records as it generated $3.79 billion in pre-orders and first-day sales.

    According to recent reports, over 93 percent of Rockstar workers across offices in Edinburgh, Leeds, Lincoln, Dundee and London took part in the two-week ballot. Of those, 1,163 turned down formal recognition of their branch of the IWGB (Independent Workers Union of Great Britain), while 381 were in favor, according to IGN.

    The Rockstar Game Workers Union will continue to organize without a formal agreement with the tech giant. However, the result means Rockstar management won't be obligated to officially recognize the union or hold regular meetings with representatives.

    "For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society — this isn't a sign to retreat, it's a sign to double down on what we stand for," the union stated in a statement. "Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favor of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognize we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We're ready to put in the effort to make that happen." It added that it will keep battling for "pay transparency, contractual overtime pay and protections against AI and layoffs.".

    "We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we've built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6," Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar Games head of publishing, said in a statement. "This result reflects our team's strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we're excited to build on all we've accomplished together.".

    Recent findings suggest that rockstar had indicated a willingness to work with its workers on unionization. "We go where the team goes," Klobe told Bloomberg for a story about the making of GTA 6. "So if they want a union, they will have a union.".

    In a recent development, in October last year, Rockstar fired dozens of workers, claiming they had shared confidential details about GTA 6 and made disparaging remarks about the company. The IWGB issued formal legal claims against Rockstar in which it accused the Take-Two subsidiary of union busting and unlawfully firing those workers. An employment tribunal heard closing evidence last week and a final judgement in the case is pending.

    #138917. From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

    From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working.
    • Sources indicate that as Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices.
    • As an apartment dweller in Latest York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.

    Sources indicate that as Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:.

    As an apartment dweller in Latest York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.

    I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).

    According to recent reports, accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.

    My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.

    I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.

    Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).

    In a recent development, last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.

    Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”.

    My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.

    The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.

    Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.

    The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.

    The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.

    Industry observers note that the primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel complications, and this thing has been a lifesaver.

    I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.

    Above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.

    I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.

    Sources indicate that to combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.

    My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.

    Sources indicate that on the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Presently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.

    The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.

    It has been revealed that since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.

    I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.

    When I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

    According to recent reports, when I need a secondary display, or I want to use my Apple Pencil in Photoshop or Illustrator, I use an iPad Pro. I used to have a dedicated Wacom monitor, but I find this much more convenient both in terms of space efficiency and ergonomics. If I’m not really leaning into hand drawing or lettering, I do most of my graphic work with a mouse, which is currently a Logitech MX Master 3S.

    To wrap up the final items, the chair is an Aeron I bought upcoming in 2003. I’ve had to repair it a few times over the years, but it’s either been things I consider wear items (wheels, armrests, gas cylinder) or Herman Miller has replaced under warranty. It was a big purchase for me at the time, but it’s ended up being a great investment. That’s Sophie draped over it, one of our four cats.

    Tucked next to my desk, behind the subwoofer under the little side table, is my home server and networking gear. The server runs Unraid and is primarily used for my Jellyfin media collection and Home Assistant. Networking is a combination of Unifi and Eero, but at some point I’d like to ditch the Amazon gear and go fully native Unifi.

    Industry observers note that I spend a lot of time in my office. It’s not just a place to edit, write, and do other Ars-y things. It’s also my rehearsal space and a place to relax and unwind when I need some me-time. Long-time readers won’t be surprised to see Apple hardware front and center. I’ve been using Macs since college, and they’ve done alright by me ever since. My daily driver is a first-gen Mac Studio (M1 Max) with 64GB of RAM, which drives two Apple Studio Displays. As a long-time mouse hater, I use a Magic Trackpad along with my extended Apple keyboard. Underneath the desk is a UPS and a Thunderbolt disk enclosure that is one of my two backups.

    The bookshelves are where my home networking gear lives. That includes a Synology DS920+ that backs up all of the computers in the house, serves up media, and runs my instance of Mealie. The Eero 6+ handles home networking, with everything in my office except my MacBook Pro connected via Ethernet. As much as I’d like to live a paperless existence, the HP printer-scanner-copier combo still gets some use. They’re difficult to see, but to the right of the G4 Cube (sadly inoperable) on top of the bookshelf sit an Apple TV and M2 Mac mini, which hook up to the 43-inch TV. My graphite iBook and eMate are now resigned to propping up bibs from races and other cycling events.

    This is my office, which is the place where I am much of the time. The chair is a Herman Miller Embody and is one of the best things I’ve ever spent money on. The desk is a standy desk that I don’t stand at nearly often enough; the work PC is a Mac Studio; and the gaming PC is a frankenbox with a cockpit running Windows 10 LTSC (from my cold dead hands, etc., etc.). The Linux boxen are headless and are mostly banished to the closet.

    Sources indicate that the paintings (including the awesome Apollo 12 SCE-to-aux one) are all originals by the inimitable Stephen Quick, who does a hell of a job with commissions. What started as a funny idea about a Warhol-esque take on the many faces of Kurt Russel kinda turned over a couple of years into somewhat of a “these are some actors whose work I like” series. My buddies and I went to a lot of movies when we were teenagers, so the imagery sparks good memories for me.

    The rest of the office has space stuff in it, especially the part behind where I was standing to do the pano sot. I’ve heard it noted that when a man hits his 40s, he must choose between becoming obsessed with World War 2 history or smoking meats; I did kind of a variation on “World War 2” and fell deeply into historic human spaceflight. Apollo is kind of my jam, and some weekends you can even catch me docenting at Space Center Houston’s Saturn V exhibit! (Yeah, it’s maybe not as pretty as the exhibits at Marshall or KSC, but the JSC Saturn V is the only one made of flight stages end to end!).

    Sources indicate that welcome to the mess of wires, monitors, and handheld fidgets that is my loft desk. Let’s take a quick tour along with the rest of my gaming cave/mid-life crisis Mario collection that lives right by it.

    Sources indicate that my office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.

    An iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.

    Absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now introduced, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who states this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

    According to recent reports, this image is a bit misleading, in that it implies I work on the pictured PC (RTX 4070, Ryzen 5 3600X, 32GB RAM) and sit at my desk while doing so. That’s occasionally true, but more often, I can be found wandering around my apartment with my M4 MacBook Air during work hours. I don’t even sit at my desk to game much anymore—on the off chance that I’m playing a game the Steam Deck can’t handle natively, I’ll stream it from my PC to my Steam Deck using Moonlight and Apollo (previously Moonlight and Sunshine).

    It has been revealed that you may also notice that my desk, from a company called Uplift, is adjustable. As it turns out, I don’t enjoy standing while working, so the ability to loft my tabletop skyward has been chiefly deployed in the service of making it easier to retrieve something I’ve dropped down there.

    Industry observers note that at night, my desk often moonlights as a craft area; I swap out my keyboard (a Wobkey Rainy75) for a cutting mat, and I’m ready to build some Gundam, assemble a book nook, or tackle a crochet pattern (a few amigurumi are scattered around my desk to keep me tech giant). You can see some of my supplies on the left, but I have other stuff stashed in drawers and various containers that I can bring to my desk as needed.

    So sure, I do work here sometimes.

    Sources indicate that my wife Anna and I rent an apartment in Chicago, and we’ve chosen the city life over, well, space. As such, my 10-by-10-foot office space serves multiple functions. I use it primarily for work, but since Anna and I are both major gamers and she is often camped out with the PlayStation 5 in the living room, I have my own gaming setup in the office. It’s cramped, but it works!

    According to recent reports, I do editing, news hits, and most other work during the day, but I’m a night owl at heart and find that I can only do heavy writing—like on longer feature articles—at night, so I’m picturing both the daytime and nighttime view here. I have a collection of Govee lights (Govee Hexa panels, several RGB Edison bulbs, and a Star Light Aurora galaxy projector) to max out the vibes for those nighttime focus (and gaming) sessions.

    We moved into this place in the dead of the pandemic, and I bought most of the stuff in this office during that year or shortly afterward, so it’s a very 2020–2021-coded array of hardware.

    In a recent development, the desk is a Secretlab Magnus Pro, and the chair is a Steelcase Gesture. I love the desk, but I have mixed feelings about the chair. I don’t like the material of the Herman Miller Aeron, but people kept telling me to buy an ergonomic chair for long-term back health, so I bought the other one everyone recommends. To be frank, I’m never fully comfortable in it, though, and wish I had just said “life is short” and bought something comfy and bad for me!

    The main machine is a 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M1 Max, 64GB of RAM, and a 2TB hard drive—still holding strong after five years. I also have an Alienware Aurora R10—hear me out—prebuilt gaming desktop with a Ryzen 9 5900X and an RTX 3080. When I bought it, it was during the COVID-times GPU shortage, and there was absolutely no other way to get the GPU I wanted. The system is loud, hot, and hard to work with; I want very much to replace it with something custom, but the need has not yet arisen. I tend to hold on to stuff until it literally stops working.

    As for monitors, the center monitor is a 27-inch, 1440p, 240 Hz OLED Asus XG27AQDMGZ. The left and right monitors are both 27-inch 4K, 60 Hz IPS Dell U2720Qs. I’ve got a pair of Audioengine A2+ speakers, plus a Blue Yeti X, a Logitech Lighta Glow, and the good ol’ Logitech C920 for video and voice calls.

    Then there’s input: a Keychron K1 Pro keyboard, a Razer Orochi V2 mouse, and a Sony DualSense controller. I’ve got a Belkin charging station for my iPhone 17 Pro, AirPods Pro, and Apple Watch Series 7, plus AirPods Max on a headphone hanger on the front of the desk. The CalDigit E5 Thunderbolt hub is doing a lot of work here!

    Recent findings suggest that I feel fortunate to have a job that allows me to occasionally apply my lifelong love affair with video games. My favorite game of all time is The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim (Morrowind is a close second), and I like Bethesda games in general. I’ve got a working (but mostly useless) Fallout Pip-Boy, which ought to count for something! I also have a few other Skyrim knickknacks hanging about. And if you’re a Star Trek: The Next Generation viewer, you might have already noticed the desk mat.

    It has been revealed that I do enjoy playing games at my desk sometimes, but after I sit at the computer all day, I often want to be somewhere else when winding down. So pictured here is the other half of the room. The leather armchair I use for console gaming is paired with a leather ottoman (the colors don’t match because, again, COVID-era supply limitations).

    I have an LG C1 OLED TV with a PlayStation 5 Pro, a PlayStation 3 that is backward-compatible with PlayStation 1 and 2 games, a Nintendo Switch I barely touch, and three Analogue FPGA retro consoles: the Super Nt, Mega Sg, and 3D.

    It’s a tiny room to spend so much time in, but after almost seven years in this apartment, it certainly feels like home!

    #138916. Tech Report: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (689 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that when Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct.
    • It has been revealed that it’s an awkward stance for a organization whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules.
    • Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that when Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

    It has been revealed that it’s an awkward stance for a organization whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

    Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

    In a recent development, “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their tech giant. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”.

    The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

    Sources indicate that “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that tech giant as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”.

    Sources indicate that plass notes companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he noted, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”.

    Sources indicate that of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession proposal, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

    “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he remarked. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”.

    Sources indicate that in that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the tech giant.

    At odds over the EU budget, European leaders cut summit short

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday, November 26, below:.
    • European Council President Antonio Costa remarked that 24 out of 27 members of the EU supported a proposal for a €45 billion loan for Ukraine.
    • That loan is split into two sections, with €20 billion to help finance for civil services and the other €25 billion going to arms and ammunition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday, November 26, below:.

    European Council President Antonio Costa remarked that 24 out of 27 members of the EU supported a proposal for a €45 billion loan for Ukraine.

    That loan is split into two sections, with €20 billion to help finance for civil services and the other €25 billion going to arms and ammunition.

    Euro News reported earlier in the day that Bulgaria reversed course and was ready to join the loan, so long as it was only paying into the part that wasn't covering Ukraine's military needs.

    European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen noted there was considerable work to be done before a deal could be in place.

    EU leaders cut short a second day of talks that was due to take place tomorrow and pushed discussions to another summit in December.

    The disagreements over a shared EU budget for the years between 2028 and 2034 stem from different priorities among EU members.

    Some countries prefer greater funding for defense and enhancing competitiveness, while others seek to keep in place funding for agriculture, among other complications.

    EU leaders ultimately weren't able to reach an agreement at the end of Thursday.

    French President Emmanuel Macron said far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen should be more humble after she criticized efforts to reach a deal on the EU budget before the end of the year.

    EU leaders were gathered in Brussels throughout the day to see if they could hammer out an agreement over a shared budget from 2028 to 2034.

    But they remain far apart on many issues, including some members opposing the use of funds for military aid to Ukraine.

    During the day, Le Pen, who is projected to beat her centrist rivals in the April 2027 elections, accused Macron and the European Commission of trying to rush through a budget deal before next year.

    "The apparent aim is to ‌deter ​us from defending France's interests in EU budget negotiations if the French people entrust us with the responsibility of governing," she remarked in a post on X.

    Industry observers note that macron hit back, saying later: "Mrs. Le Pen is campaigning. It takes a peculiar kind ​of arrogance to think she’s already in charge ​of France's destiny. ‌Last I checked, she wasn’t elected.".

    Macron said he was careful to take into account the presidential election and that if there was no deal by December 31, negotiations would have to resume in the second half of 2027, when his successor would be in office.

    "You have to be more humble when you're campaigning, even if you already see yourself in the job," Macron mentioned.

    EU leaders hadn't made as much progress in their discussions about the EU's next long-term budget, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten remarked.

    Jetten said it was up to EU Council President Antonio Costa to come up with an improvised proposal for the next budget, which he said would be debated in "more intense" negotiations in December.

    EU leaders are still hoping to have another round of talks around midnight before calling it a day.

    Like Germany, the Netherlands is a net contributor to the European Union.

    German Chancellor Friedrich Merz mentioned EU leaders will try to reach an agreement on the next multi-annual budget for the EU by the end of this year.

    Merz said a day of talks among EU leaders in Brussels had brought "upcoming movement" toward a reduction of the proposed size of the next budget, as demanded by Germany and other countries that are net contributors to the bloc's finances.

    The leaders will try to hammer out a deal during a two-day summit starting December 17, Merz said.

    Germany has been leading calls to attach a durable funding scheme for Ukraine to the EU's next budget.

    Merz has made clear that his country would approve the next budget if all countries backed a loan for Ukraine.

    Last year, the EU reached an agreement on a €90 billion loan to Ukraine through a compromise loan after a much-discussed frozen-asset strategy failed.

    The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia opted out of backing the loan.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Contrary to earlier expectations, European Union leaders weren't quite done for the day, even if it was well past 2200 local time.

    German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stated that rather than meet again as scheduled on Friday, leaders would hold a final round of discussions around midnight and end the summit.

    Thank you for reading along with our coverage of the Euro Summit on Thursday.

    We will be back tomorrow to bring you the latest from the second day.

    Until then, you can watch DW's analysis of the event:.

    Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has said the chances of reaching an agreement on Thursday are "virtually zero.".

    Leaders of the European Union are gathered today in Brussels to agree on the bloc's budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.

    In an X post, Magyar mentioned he outlined "Hungary’s priorities and the red lines" to the other member states.

    "Having heard the completely opposing positions around the table, I would put the chances of reaching an agreement today at virtually zero," he wrote.

    He also mentioned "an agreement around Christmas looks unlikely" as well.

    Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez celebrated "a Spain that leads in Europe like never before," after the nomination of Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the next European Central Bank (ECB) chief.

    Hernandez de Cos is set to become the upcoming ECB head as the European Union (EU) leaders are gathered in Brussels for the Euro Summit.

    Sanchez welcomed the news in a post on X, pointing out that the top EU positions held by Spanish officials Teresa Ribera, the European Commission's First Executive Vice-President, and Nadia Calvino, head of the European Investment Bank.

    "In short, Spain leads in Europe like never before," he wrote.

    Spanish candidate Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the next president of the European Central Bank (ECB), after being endorsed by the majority ‌of ​eurozone countries, news agencies reported.

    In a recent development, as the leaders gather for the Euro Summit, the Financial Times first reported that de Cos will be the next ECB chief, citing ​people ​familiar with ​the matter. This was confirmed by Reuters and AFP, citing EU diplomat sources.

    The decision came after the Netherlands stated it would support the Spaniard as a consensus candidate.

    Christine Lagarde has been president since November 2019 but has declared her intention to step down on February 7, 2027.

    De Cos was up against Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot for the presidency, while France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier have been nominated for the ECB's two other top jobs.

    Russia has criticized the European Union's proposed seven-year budget, accusing the bloc of seeking to prolong the war in Ukraine.

    Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov noted the EU's aims to allocate money for Ukraine in its budget would make Kyiv "less inclined toward a peace process and more determined to continue the war.".

    Peskov said the result would be more military spending, leaving less for governments to spend on school, hospitals and social facilities.

    "This is not money for peace," Peskov remarked.

    Support for Ukraine is among the key areas of discussion in the 2028-2034 budget which includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, however diplomats say this figure falls well short of Kyiv's needs.

    Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has added her voice to those warning that European leaders have their work cut out for them when it comes to agreeing on a multi-year budget proposal.

    "We're light-years ‌away from a ‌solution," ​Meloni told reporters ahead of the EU summit in Brussels.

    "We are not willing ⁠to ​sign off ​on a budget ​under which ‌we would have to ​give ⁠more to receive less," ⁠she ​added.

    Earlier, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz mentioned the budget was "still too high" and that members states needed to be able to afford the full cost without taking on upcoming debt.

    Last week, European Council President Antonio Costa presented a new compromise proposal of €1.78 trillion ($1.95 trillion), around €204 billion lower than the initial proposal by the European Commission.

    It has been revealed that every seven years, European leaders gather in Brussels for what is arguably the most consequential negotiation cycle in the European Union. As German Chancellor Friedrich Merz put it upon arrival, it is about "the future of the European Union.".

    Industry observers note that this is not a typical EU summit. The leaders of the 27 member states are confronting a question that will shape all angles of EU politics for years to come: How much money should the EU have, who should pay for it, and what should it be spent on?

    It is the essence of EU summit diplomacy: a painstaking exercise in give-and-take, bargaining and compromise.

    The European Commission laid down the opening bid over the summer. The proposal was ambitious. Brussels wants an EU budget that reflects a rapidly-changing world: more spending on defence, innovation, research, digital technologies and competitiveness. At the same time, that inevitably means pressure on some of the traditional pillars of EU spending, particularly agricultural subsidies and parts of the bloc's regional development programmes.

    Since then, every member has arrived with a shopping list of demands.

    Governments have pushed back against cuts, demanded new priorities, sought exemptions and fought for national interests. There have though also been others who are pushing FOR a reduction in spending, including Merz.

    The original proposal from Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has already undergone numerous adjustments as negotiators attempted to accommodate competing demands.

    The result is an extraordinarily complex puzzle.

    At the centre of it all stands European Council President Antonio Costa. He will be shuttling between bilateral meetings with leaders, gather small groups behind closed doors and attempt to construct a package that gives everybody something they can take home and present as a victory.

    According to recent reports, for Costa, the stakes are high. Delivering an agreement would be a major test of his authority and reputation as the EU's chief broker. Especially as he was not made top negotiator for the EU in the peace talks on Russia's war in Ukraine. Diplomats expressed confidence in his fairness and negotiating skills before the summit, viewing him as someone capable of building trust among leaders who have differing priorities.

    Yet nobody in Brussels expects an easy breakthrough. Many officials acknowledge that the pressure on member states may not yet be intense enough to force the final concessions required for a deal. Leaders are still defending red lines rather than crossing them.

    So, this summit will highly likely end without a grand agreement. Leaders will probably decide to take stock of the latest negotiating proposals and return home to assess them in detail. There will be a latest — and perhaps final — round on the next summit in December, a few days before Christmas.

    As leaders grapple with long-term budgets, across Europe, young people are rising up. They're demanding better jobs, more funding for education and lower rents. The problems they are protesting are complex and often specific to their home country.

    It has been revealed that but there’s also a common message: Young people feel pessimistic about their economic future. A look at the data shows they could be right.

    Bulgaria's Prime Minister Rumen Radev remarked his country would support a proposed €45 billion ($49 billion) EU loan to Ukraine, but only the funds earmarked for non-military aid.

    "Bulgaria is going to take part ​in the loan of €20 billion (for) non-military support for Ukraine," ⁠Radev ​told reporters as he arrived ​at the EU summit in Brussels.

    According to recent reports, "We ​have a ‌huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living in Ukraine, our wish ​is ⁠to concentrate our support in that area. ⁠We are ​going to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons," Radev mentioned.

    Last week European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen noted the €45 billion would be split into two parts: ‌up to €25 billion for military aid and up to €20 billion for other ‌help as a means of getting member states to contribute where there were objections to funding weapons for Ukraine.

    German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 was "still too too high" and did not provide the basis for an agreement, during comments made as he arrived at the summit.

    "After all, the member states must be able ​to afford to pay for ⁠all ​of this," Merz remarked in Brussels.

    ​The German leader also remarked the war in Ukraine needed to be ended as soon as possible and that the country needed help during a "very difficult winter.".

    Merz remarked that funding for Kyiv is "a task that we must also accomplish together,” and added: "The European Union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24.".

    Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Hungary have been exempt from contributing to aid for Ukraine. The countries negotiated, as part of the current €90 billion loan for Ukraine, that they would not have financial obligations in guaranteeing the loan.

    Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis did not agree with the German chancellor.

    "Funding for Ukraine should be negotiated separately," stated Babis, adding that his country needs the money for other expenditures. "I believe we will fight for this money," providing an early indication of how talks might proceed over the next two days.

    Beijing claims new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’.

    Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU.

    Beijing has stated it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.

    Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
